newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Refugee invasion launched from Albanian beaches.
newsitem.headline: Refugee invasion launched from Albanian beaches.

text.p: A woman with a child in her arms balanced precariously on Monday on the sloping wall of a breakwater jutting out into the Adriatic from a beach in Albania.
She tried to hand the child down to a motorboat bobbing in the sea but the two men on board were too busy to help.
One waved a Kalashnikov with a fixed bayonet to keep unauthorized passengers at bay. The other worked the motor and an oar, struggling furiously to keep the boat in place.
The woman and child were in danger of toppling into the sea, but a man pushed them aside and lifted his large German Shepherd dog into the boat and then climbed in himself.
Three other men clambered on board and they finally helped the poor woman and her child. Then boat pushed off from the breakwater and headed out towards a line of rusting skows on the horizon.
All the Albanians, would-be refugees, had paid the equivalent of $250 each for a chance to get to Italy by boat.
Hundreds of paying passengers crouched on the breakwater and pier at Agip beach, south of Durres, waiting for small boats to shuttle them out to the refugee ships.
Another thousand or so milled around on the beach in the shadow of a grounded and derelict freighter, trying to worm their way onto the breakwater without paying.
Surly men in civilian clothes, some in ski masks, prevented them from advancing by repeatedly firing rifle rounds over their heads while screaming curses and threats.
The shots panicked young children and infants whose terrified bawling added to the chaotic atmosphere. Every few minutes the gunmen would drive the crowd back only to have it press forward again.
"Go away, go away. Only those people who paid their money will be able to leave from here," the guards shouted.
One man who arrived on the beach by taxi with his wife, three children and two small bags looked bewildered.

"We want to go to Italy but we have no idea how to get out," said Hasan, 57. "The situation in Durres is frightening. There are too many guns. I have no job. We have no house. We lost our money in the investment schemes."
The collapse of five pyramid schemes left many families destitute and Albania is in an advanced state of lawlessness, especially in the south.
A new coalition government is working with international mediators to try to restore order but many people remain convinced that the only solution is to flee.

Most offers to leave Albania by boat are no more savory than the pyramid schemes which precipitated the crisis. The boatlifts appear to be controlled by local mafia groups, sometimes working in league with the police.
Ten uniformed policemen cleared Agip beach at one point on Monday by walking in a phalanx through the sand behind a van and firing their Kalashnikovs into the air.
At the breakwater, instead of disarming the gunmen sowing terror there, they mixed freely with them and then drove away in their van.
One of the gunmen strutted up the beach to a comrade and confided within earshot of journalists: "There's a problem.
"We're loading these people but the military is out there in ships. I don't know whether it's the Albanians or the Italians, but somebody's not letting our boats take the people across."
He did not bother to convey this message to the people queuing on the breakwater or waiting anxiously on the beach. Probably no one would have believed him anyway.
